passages.text: RESPIRATION, the act of breathing, by which the air is alternately drawn into the lungs and driven out of them.
Inspiration is performed by the descent of the diaphragm and the raising of the ribs, by which the cavity of the chest is enlarged and the air rushes in.
The ancients believed that the use of respiration was to cool the blood; which opinion is still held by some.

But Mr Lavoisier has shown that in respiration the vital air is absorbed, and fixed air is given out, in the same manner as in the burning of charcoal; so that respiration is a slow combustion carried on in the lungs, which is the source of animal heat.
A man breathes about twenty times in a minute.
The blood which has passed through the lungs changes from a dark to a florid red colour.
Breathing is the process of moving air into and out of the lungs to allow gas exchange, mostly to take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and moves down and the rib cage is raised, enlarging the chest cavity so that air flows in.
In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. Blood rich in oxygen is bright red; blood low in oxygen is darker.
Cells use the oxygen in cellular respiration to release energy from food, producing carbon dioxide and water. Much of this energy is released as body heat.
A resting adult breathes about 12 to 20 times a minute.
Breathing is controlled automatically by the brainstem, which responds mainly to the level of carbon dioxide in the blood.
Lavoisier's experiments in the 1770s and 1780s showed that respiration consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, like combustion.

reasons: The 1797 entry is about breathing, which Wikipedia covers under Breathing.
Rare terms appear in both: diaphragm, ribs, Lavoisier, colour of the blood.
Cellular respiration scores on the headword but covers chemistry inside cells, not breathing.

suggestedQuestions: Why did people in 1797 think we breathe?
Was Lavoisier right that breathing is a kind of burning?

Why did people in 1797 think we breathe?.answer: The entry gives two views. The old one, still held by some, was that breathing cools the blood [B3]. The newer one, from Lavoisier, was that breathing takes in vital air and gives out fixed air, like burning charcoal [B4]. Wikipedia matches the newer view: we breathe to take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide [W1].

Was Lavoisier right that breathing is a.answer: Largely. The 1797 entry reports his view of a slow combustion that produces animal heat, placed in the lungs [B4]. Wikipedia says cells use the oxygen to release energy from food, much of it as body heat [W4]. The difference is the place: the cells, not the lungs.
